briefs.headline: CERT-In seeks checks on access of AI agents
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India's cybersecurity agency has called for testing whether AI agents can leak confidential data or take unauthorised actions, putting permissions and human oversight at the centre of its audit guidelines.
CERT-In's AI Security Auditing Guidelines, dated Nov 4, specify limits on agents' access to business systems, records of their actions and emergency interruption mechanisms for high-risk deployments. Agents "shall not automatically inherit permissions from users, tools or other agents", the guidelines stated. The safeguards address prompt injection, where malicious instructions hidden in documents or other inputs attempt to hijack an AI system's behaviour.
"Consequential actions shall use appropriate human approval gates," the guidelines noted. Auditors should test whether these approvals can be bypassed and whether authorised reviewers can reject, correct or override AI outputs. The framework also calls for testing safeguards against data leaks.

briefs.headline: Adani Ports to buy storage operator Evos for $2.9bn
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone (APSEZ) has agreed to acquire 100% of Netherlands-based Evos BV from Igneo Infrastructure Partners at an enterprise value of $2.9bn, marking a major expansion of its international operations and giving it a significant presence in Europe's liquid storage and energy infrastructure market.
The proposed all-cash transaction values Evos at an equity value of $1.3bn and an enterprise value-to-ebitda multiple of 11.7 times based on its calendar year 2025 financial performance, APSEZ said in a statement.
The acquisition will give APSEZ control of eight port-based liquid storage terminals across the Netherlands, Germany, Spain, Belgium and Malta.
Evos, Europe's second-largest independent liquid storage operator, has a total storage capacity of 6.3 million cubic metres and handled 37 million tonne of throughput in CY25. It reported a revenue of $440 million and ebitda of $246 million during the year, translating into an ebitda margin of 56%.
The acquisition will expand APSEZ's global network to 28 ports and terminals across 10 countries, strengthening its position as an integrated transport and logistics operator while diversifying its exposure across geographies and cargo segments.
The transaction will be funded through debt and is subject to regulatory and other approvals, as well as works council consultation. MUFG is the sole underwriter and has provided financing commitments of up to $3.2 billion for the proposed acquisition.
Evos operates eight terminals with 452 storage tanks, 63 vessel and barge berths and multiple pipeline connections across five European countries. Its facilities are located in major energy and industrial centres.

stories.headline: ‘He reads situation earlier than others’: India coach on Kohli's fielding brilliance
stories.deck: Subhadeep Ghosh, India's fielding coach, lauded the team's dedication in their recent ODI triumph over New Zealand. They effectively confined New Zealand to 185 runs, demonstrating exceptional fielding prowess. Key contributions came from senior players Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma, who displayed remarkable anticipation and agile movements. Ghosh emphasized the need to adapt to varying overseas…
stories.bodyText:
India fielding coach Subhadeep Ghosh has praised the team's sharpness and commitment on the field following their victory in the opening ODI against New Zealand, pointing to the collective effort of the fielding unit in restricting the hosts to 185.
India began the five-match series with a five-wicket win via the DLS method in a rain-interrupted contest at Eden Park in Auckland on Wednesday. Ghosh felt the team's performance in the field, particularly their catching, ground fielding and overall intensity, complemented the bowlers' efforts in keeping New Zealand's total under control.
Speaking to reporters on the eve of the second ODI in Hamilton, Ghosh expressed satisfaction with the way the players backed up the bowling attack with their fielding contributions.
"We did well in the first ODI. We took some good catches, picked up wickets and backed it up with excellent ground fielding. The intensity was very good. When you restrict the opposition to around 180, it reflects not just good bowling but also quality fielding," Ghosh said.
Among the standout moments in the series opener were 
Virat Kohli
's spectacular catch and 
Rohit Sharma
's sharp run-out. Both senior batters made significant contributions in the field, with Ghosh attributing their efforts to their ability to anticipate situations and read the game quickly.
Explaining 
Kohli
's brilliance, the fielding coach pointed to the batter's extensive experience in the cover and point positions, which allows him to judge the direction and movement of the ball more effectively.
"I think anticipation is extremely important. The more time you spend in a particular fielding position, the better you become at reading the game. Virat has fielded at cover and point countless times, so he knows the trajectory and path of the ball, as well as how it is likely to travel after impact. He reads the situation slightly earlier than others, and you can see that in his execution," he said.
Ghosh also broke down Rohit's contribution to the run-out, explaining how the Indian batter had already begun moving towards square leg after anticipating where the ball was likely to travel. That early movement helped him execute the dismissal with precision.
"As far as Rohit is concerned, I think he anticipated that the ball would go towards square leg during that run-out. He wasn't moving straight; he was already shifting slightly towards square leg. That early anticipation allowed him to execute the skill perfectly. The more familiar you become with a particular position, the quicker you are able to anticipate what is going to happen. That's what makes the difference," he added.
The fielding coach also spoke about the difficulties players encounter while adjusting to different playing conditions during overseas tours. Varying ground dimensions, colder weather and unfamiliar boundary placements can all influence a fielder's positioning and movement.
According to Ghosh, understanding the dimensions of a ground and making the correct initial movement are particularly important, as they help players cover more ground and reduce the angles available to opposition batters.
"When you travel to different countries, adapting to new conditions is always a challenge. The ground dimensions vary, the weather can be cold, and these are aspects we regularly discuss in the dressing room. In terms of ground dimensions, when you field in a particular position, observing the batters and understanding where the boundary rope is becomes important. Your first step is crucial because it allows you to cut down the angles and cover the ground more effectively.
 We constantly work on that initial movement," he said.
Ghosh further stressed that adapting to changing environments is an essential part of international cricket and requires players to maintain the right approach, irrespective of whether they are training or competing.
"That is part of the challenge of international cricket. You travel to different countries, encounter different conditions and have to adapt accordingly. With optional training sessions, it ultimately comes down to your mindset. I always emphasise the importance of having the right mindset, both individually and as a group," he concluded.
India will take on New Zealand in the second ODI at Seddon Park in Hamilton on Saturday. While the hosts will be eager to draw level, India will look to build on their opening victory and extend their advantage in the series.

stories.headline: ‘Ordinary bowler’: Ex-cricketer slams CSK's 'confusing' trade, says SRH real winners
stories.deck: Kris Srikkanth has raised concerns regarding Chennai Super Kings' recent trades involving Liam Livingstone and Jack Edwards. He contends that Sunrisers Hyderabad emerged as the true winners of the four-player exchange ahead of the IPL 2027 auction. Srikkanth examined Livingstone's potential role in CSK's squad and expressed skepticism over acquiring Edwards, noting that existing overseas talents…
stories.bodyText:
Former India opener 
Kris Srikkanth
 has questioned 
Chennai Super Kings
' decision to trade for 
Liam Livingstone
 and Jack Edwards, believing Sunrisers Hyderabad have emerged as the bigger winners from the four-player deal ahead of the IPL 2027 auction.
CSK and SRH completed the trade on Thursday, with England all-rounder Livingstone and Australian seam-bowling all-rounder Edwards moving to the five-time champions. In exchange, India pacer Khaleel Ahmed and Australian fast bowler Nathan Ellis joined SRH.
Reacting to the development on his YouTube channel, Srikkanth was particularly critical of CSK's decision to bring Edwards on board, describing the Australian as an ordinary bowler. He also questioned whether Livingstone would have a clear role in the Chennai side.
"Why Jack Edwards? He is an ordinary bowler. I am okay with CSK giving away Khaleel Ahmed as he's nothing great. This trade is a better one for SRH. Personally, I think Livingstone is a good cricketer if utilised well. But how he fits in with CSK is a big question mark. CSK should release Matt Short, who is a waste, and see if Livingstone can be an upgrade for him," said Srikkanth.
Edwards, who made his international debut for Australia in January this year, will join CSK at his existing contract value of Rs 3 crore. SRH had signed him before his international debut, but the all-rounder did not get an opportunity to feature in IPL 2026 after a foot injury forced him out of the tournament.
Livingstone, meanwhile, will move to CSK for Rs 6 crore, a significant reduction from the Rs 13 crore at which SRH had originally acquired him.
Srikkanth's concerns about the deal also stem from the overseas-player combination available to CSK. With franchises permitted to field a maximum of four overseas players in their playing XI, he believes Livingstone could find it difficult to secure a regular place.
The former India opener pointed out that CSK already have three overseas players who are likely to feature regularly, leaving limited room for the England all-rounder.
"CSK already have three sure starters among their overseas players in Dewald Brevis, Noor Ahmad and Jamie Overton. So Livingstone can only be the fourth option, and even there, CSK could go with Akeal Hosein. It's a very confusing trade and not a convincing trade for CSK. Will CSK benefit from this? It's a big question mark. I am not convinced by Edwards either, and his domestic track record is also nothing great. So this trade definitely favors SRH," Srikkanth added.
While Livingstone's ability to contribute with both bat and ball could offer CSK another option, Srikkanth remains unconvinced about how the two incoming players fit into the team's plans. He believes the exchange has given SRH a more favourable deal heading into the IPL 2027 auction.

briefs.headline: ‘I faced lot of hate’: RCB star reveals how he was trolled whenever Gill hit a ton
briefs.deck: Venkatesh Iyer experienced significant online backlash from Kolkata Knight Riders supporters after Shubman Gill's release. Fans would often criticize him on social media whenever Gill performed well. He revealed his thoughts about his situation ahead of the IPL 2026 auction, mentioning his previous approach to Shah Rukh Khan. After being released, Iyer moved on and joined Royal Challengers…
briefs.bodyText:
Venkatesh Iyer
 has opened up about the prolonged online backlash he faced from Kolkata Knight Riders (KKR) supporters following the franchise's decision to retain him while releasing 
Shubman Gill
 ahead of IPL 2022. The Royal Challengers Bengaluru (RCB) batter revealed that the criticism has continued over the years, with fans still targeting him whenever Gill scores a century.
Gill was released by KKR ahead of the 2022 season and subsequently became one of the three players drafted by the newly formed Gujarat Titans (GT), who secured his services for Rs 8 crore alongside 
Hardik Pandya
 and Rashid Khan.
Speaking in a podcast with Aakash Chopra, Venkatesh recalled how KKR supporters have repeatedly brought up the franchise's decision, making him a target of social media trolling.
"I have been subject to a lot of hate for a long time. Even till date, if Shubman is getting a hundred; you go to a KKR page, people would be commenting, 'in search of gold, we lost a diamond' and all of that stuff," Venkatesh said.
The 31-year-old also discussed his situation ahead of the IPL 2026 auction, particularly after KKR decided to release him. He revealed that he had even approached franchise co-owner Shah Rukh Khan in the hope of a change in the decision.
"I had kept an hankerchief on the side. I even asked Shah Rukh sir," he said.
KKR had spent Rs 23.75 crore to buy Venkatesh back ahead of the 2025 season. However, following his release, the all-rounder admitted that he had already moved on mentally and was not even considering a return to the franchise during the 2026 auction.
"I didn't even think about the pay cut. I had already started thinking, 'Okay, it's not going to be purple'," he said.
Venkatesh was eventually signed by defending champions RCB, where he got an opportunity to experience a completely different fan culture. The batter was particularly struck by the devotion of Bengaluru supporters and described their connection with the franchise as something he had never witnessed before.
"You won't believe this, but I saw people actually worshipping the RCB jersey before matches. This was something different. Fandom at a different level," Venkatesh recalled.
His initial days at RCB involved spending time on the bench before he was introduced as an Impact Substitute after the team suffered an early collapse in the batting order. He responded with an unbeaten 29 off 15 deliveries, helping RCB reach 201/8, although the team eventually lost the match.
Venkatesh later delivered another impressive performance against Punjab Kings, remaining unbeaten on 73 off 40 balls.
He ended the season with 209 runs from seven matches at an average of 52.25, playing his part in RCB's successful campaign as the franchise secured its second IPL title in a row.

briefs.headline: Big blow for NZ! Star batter ruled out of remainder of ODI series against India
briefs.deck: Devon Conway will miss the ODI series against India due to a concussion injury, making way for Nick Kelly to step in. Kelly is set to join the team in Wellington by Friday. In a positive update, Matt Henry has been declared free of concussion after a training incident. New Zealand faced defeat in the first ODI, despite a strong performance from Virat Kohli.
briefs.bodyText:
New Zealand have suffered a setback ahead of the second ODI against India, with opener Devon Conway ruled out of the remaining matches of the five-game series after sustaining a concussion during a training session on Tuesday.
Conway suffered the injury while fielding during practice, forcing him out of the remainder of the ODI series. Left-handed batter Nick Kelly, who was initially selected for the fourth and fifth ODIs, will now join the squad in Wellington on Friday as his replacement.
There was some relief for the New Zealand camp, however, as Matt Henry, who was involved in the fielding mishap that resulted in Conway's injury, has been cleared of concussion.
The development comes after New Zealand lost the opening ODI to India in Auckland on Wednesday. 
Virat Kohli
's authoritative 74, coupled with impressive bowling performances from Arshdeep Singh and Anshul Kamboj, helped India secure a comfortable victory in the rain-affected contest.
Arshdeep led the attack with four wickets, while Gurnoor Brar picked up three scalps and Kamboj claimed two as New Zealand were bowled out for 185. India then chased down the revised target of 143 in 32 overs despite rain interruptions.
The second ODI will be played at Sky Stadium in Wellington on Saturday, with New Zealand looking to bounce back and level the series.

briefs.headline: 'The drivers are here': India's next generation of racers dream of an F1 breakthrough
briefs.deck: Saishiva Sankaran and Viswas Vijayaraj underline the challenges young Indian racers face in pursuing a career in motorsport, with limited testing, financial constraints and the demands of balancing education and racing. As they target Formula 1, both stress the need for greater support for Indian drivers to compete on the international stage. Their return to the Buddh International Circuit also…
briefs.bodyText:
In a country where cricket dominates the sporting landscape, motorsport continues to fight for attention. For young Indian racers, reaching Formula 1 remains the ultimate ambition, but the path to the top comes with financial constraints, limited opportunities and sacrifices away from the track.
For Saishiva Sankaran and Viswas Vijayaraj, that path began with a childhood love for cars and racing. Speaking to Times of India during the Indian Racing Festival's return to the Buddh International Circuit after 13 years, the two drivers spoke about their careers, the demands of competing against international racers and what it takes to pursue a career in motorsport in India.
From karting in Pune to the Indian Racing League
Saishiva Sankaran began racing when he was eight years old. His interest in cars introduced him to karting at a small facility in Kharadi, Pune, where he started competing in four-stroke karting events. He won his first event before moving to two-stroke karting, gaining experience through several championships while working with teams such as M-Sport and Kamehko Kartopia in Bengaluru.
From karting, he progressed to single-seater racing before moving into the F2000 Championship and eventually the Indian Racing League, where he represents the Kolkata Royal Tigers.
"It has been a long journey of 10 years, starting from the basics. I would like to thank my family and friends for making this possible," Sankaran said.
For Vijayaraj, who represents Chennai Turbo Riders in the Indian Racing League, the motivation came from his childhood interest in cars and racing. Representing India at the highest level remains a central part of his ambition.
"It's not just about choosing Indian motorsport, it's about the love for cars and the love for the sport which I have had since I was a kid. Since I am from India, obviously I need to represent my country at the highest level," Vijayaraj said.
The sacrifices behind a career in motorsport
Balancing racing with education and personal life has been one of Sankaran's biggest challenges. Racing calendars can leave young drivers with little time for school, college and family, particularly once the season gets underway.
"There is a lot of missing out on the schooling side and a lot of missing out on college nowadays. These events are not like tennis or cricket, where you have to practise every day. But when the season starts, it becomes quite hectic," he explained.
Preparation continues even when he is away from the circuit.
"There's a lot of training and restrictions on diet on the other side. And I also practise a lot on the simulator. When I am off track, I basically practise on the simulator trying to improve for the season," he added.
Limited testing, learning from international drivers
Competing against international drivers in the Indian Racing League has given Sankaran an opportunity to learn from racers with experience across different circuits and conditions.
"I am learning a lot from the international drivers as well. These guys have raced everywhere and in different conditions, while I have been limited mostly to India," he said.
"But there is a lot I have learned from these guys, which has helped me push on and reach the podium," he added.
Vijayaraj pointed to the difference in testing opportunities available to Indian and international drivers. While overseas competitors often get regular time on the track, Indian racers have to work around much more limited practice schedules.
"In India, we have very limited testing, unlike international drivers, who have already been on the track almost every day or most days of the week. We get to do that only for a couple of days a month," Vijayaraj said.
He believes Indian drivers can still compete with their international counterparts despite the difference in preparation time.
"For us, competing against them is a huge learning curve. It doesn't mean that we are really off them. We are on par with them. Learning from them and then being able to compete against them, or even win against them, is always the best feeling, especially with the minimum amount of practice we get," he added.
Financial backing remains a hurdle on the road to F1
Moving through the junior racing categories and getting closer to Formula 1 requires considerable financial backing. Vijayaraj acknowledged that the financial realities of the sport, coupled with age, can make it difficult for drivers to continue progressing.
"Formula 1 is always a dream. But at times, when age catches up or reality hits, it becomes really difficult because we struggle with finances and everything. That is the only support which we don't get enough," Vijayaraj said.
He believes India already has drivers capable of competing at a higher level but needs to do more to support them.
"There are a lot of experienced and really good Indian drivers who are capable of showcasing India at the highest level possible in the world. The drivers are here. You can see them on the grid right now. They just need enough support from the country so that they can represent India internationally," he added.
Sankaran, meanwhile, is looking at the next steps in his career. Having competed in Indian F4 last year, he wants to progress through the junior categories and eventually reach Formula 1. He is also looking for sponsors and brands willing to back his ambitions.
"So, I am looking to go up the ranks and reach the F1 ladder. Obviously, next year I am looking for getting sponsors and brands to, you know, invest in me and be the face of me when I reach F1. So, main goal is F1," Sankaran said.
The youngster is also a big admirer of Max Verstappen, whose aggressive driving style influenced his interest in Formula 1.
"I am a big fan of Max Verstappen. And I have taken his number. Number 33 every time I race, I have been loving him. Loving his driving style, his aggression ever since I started watching. And he is the main reason why I started watching as well," Sankaran concluded.
Buddh International Circuit: A special return for Indian racers
Racing returned to the Buddh International Circuit after 13 years, giving Indian drivers an opportunity to compete at the country's only Formula 1-grade circuit. For Vijayaraj, the weekend brought back memories of watching some of the sport's biggest names race at the venue.
He had previously competed at the circuit during the National Championship in 2019. Returning after six years was a special experience.
"Walking down the pits and everything, it is just like collecting the memories from television of where the greatest drivers like Michael Schumacher, Lewis Hamilton and Sebastian Vettel used to walk around here and race," he said.
"Being here is the best feeling an Indian driver could ever have. Coming back here after six years is the best feeling ever. It is like bringing back all the memories and reliving them again."
Vijayaraj also believes a Formula 1 return to India could generate greater interest in motorsport and open up opportunities for local drivers.
"Formula 1 coming back to India right now would be three times better than what it was back then. We have a lot of Indian fans watching racing series. Bringing Formula 1 back would be a huge boost for the entire country and could create a lot of opportunities and championships in the future," he added.
Aryan Narola, Ruhaan Alva headline Indian Racing Festival weekend
The Indian Racing Festival concluded its two-day Buddh International Circuit (BIC) leg in Greater Noida on November 1, 2026, with Aryan Narola and Ruhaan Alva emerging as the standout performers in the F4 Indian Championship and Indian Racing League (IRL), respectively.
Representing Goa Aces JA Racing, Narola secured a double victory in Sunday's two F4 races. He finished ahead of Aris Kyriakou and Ntiyiso Mabunda in the first race before beating Arjun Chheda and Mabunda in the second.
Alva of Kichcha's Kings Bengaluru won the second IRL race after capitalising on Shane Chanderia's car trouble. Mohamed Ryan of Hyderabad Blackbirds finished second, while Malaysian racer Alister Yoong of Speed Demons Delhi secured third place.
The action began on Saturday with the opening IRL and F4 races. Raoul Hyman of Goa Aces JA Racing won the opening IRL race in 27:40.759, with Saishiva Sankaran of Kolkata Royal Tigers finishing second in 27:55.806 and Jemma Moore of Kichcha's Kings Bengaluru taking third in 27:56.070.
In the opening F4 race, Ntiyiso Mabunda of Speed Demons Delhi claimed victory in 32:46.842, followed by fellow South African Luviwe Sambudla of Goa Aces JA Racing in second place and Aryan Narola in third.
Sunday's second IRL race saw Alva claim victory, followed by Mohamed Ryan in second and Alister Yoong in third.

briefs.headline: India beats Pakistan in SAFF Championship opener
briefs.deck: Suhail Ahmad Bhat scored in the 13th and 19th minutes while Manglenthang Kipgen struck in the 31st minute as India led 3-0 at half time
briefs.bodyText:
Suhail Ahmad Bhat struck a brace as defending champion India began its SAFF Championship campaign with a 3-2 victory over Pakistan in a Group B match on Thursday (November 5, 2026).
Bhat scored in the 13th and 19th minutes while Manglenthang Kipgen struck in the 31st minute as India led 3-0 at half time.
Pakistan scored two goals in the stoppage time through Najeeb Ullah and Alamgir Ghazi.
Coach Naushad Moosa had only 17 players at his disposal for Thursday’s (November 5, 2026) match as the ISL clubs are yet to release some of their players for the tournament with the game not falling in the FIFA match window (November 9 to 17).
The clubs are expected to release their players for the next match against Maldives on November 11.
The result:
India 3 (Suhail Ahmad Bhat 13, 19; Manglenthang Kipgen 31) bt Pakistan 2 (Najeeb Ullah 90+1, Alamgir Ghazi 90+4).

briefs.headline: Tanvi scripts history, becomes first Indian woman to win Youth Olympics badminton medal
briefs.deck: In a remarkable achievement at the Youth Olympic Games, Tanvi Patri has secured a historic silver medal in badminton, becoming the first Indian woman to earn a medal at the event. Competing fiercely, she reached the finals, facing off against China's Zhang Yi Xin. Although she narrowly missed out on victory, her unwavering spirit and determination shone through, amplifying India's growing…
briefs.bodyText:
At just 15, Odisha's Tanvi Patri becomes the first Indian woman to win a badminton medal at the Youth Olympic Games. Her remarkable silver-medal run in Dakar was a story of composure, courage and extraordinary fighting spirit, highlighted by a stunning comeback in the final against China's reigning World Junior Champion Zhang Yi Xin.
India's Tanvi Patri scripted a historic chapter in Indian badminton after clinching the silver medal in the women's singles event at the 2026 Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal. The 15-year-old from Odisha became the first Indian woman to reach a badminton final and win a medal at the Youth Olympics, marking a significant milestone for the country's junior badminton circuit.
However, the road to the podium was anything but straightforward. Tanvi's campaign was defined by her ability to rise to the occasion, particularly in the knockout stages, where she displayed remarkable composure against some of the tournament's strongest opponents.
The young shuttler eventually settled for silver after an 82-minute battle against China's reigning World Junior Champion Zhang Yi Xin in the gold-medal match. Tanvi went down 15-21, 21-13, 24-26 in a thrilling three-game encounter, but her spirited fightback in the deciding game ensured that her performance would be remembered long after the final point.
A fightback that nearly produced gold
The final against Zhang was a test of Tanvi's temperament and endurance. After losing the opening game 15-21, the Indian bounced back impressively to take the second game 21-13 and force a decider.
The third game, however, appeared to be slipping away from her when she found herself trailing 10-19. With the gold medal seemingly within Zhang's grasp, Tanvi produced an extraordinary response, refusing to surrender despite the mounting pressure.
She saved five consecutive match points to draw level at 24-24, turning what looked like a comfortable finish for the Chinese shuttler into a tense battle. Tanvi even earned three opportunities to seal the gold medal herself, but Zhang held her nerve in the closing exchanges to eventually prevail 26-24.
Although the defeat denied her the gold, Tanvi's determination to fight until the very end stood out as one of the defining moments of the tournament.
Tanvi Patri's road to the Youth Olympics final
The 15-year-old, who trains at the Prakash Padukone Badminton Academy (PPBA), entered the competition as the third seed and enjoyed a strong start in the group stage.
Quarterfinal: A historic semifinal entry
Tanvi faced Thailand's seventh-seeded Kakanik Kungkaew in the quarterfinals, with a place in the medal rounds at stake. The Indian youngster delivered a composed performance, winning 21-17, 21-13 in just 39 minutes. The straight-games victory not only secured her a semifinal berth but also made her the first Indian woman to reach the badminton semifinals at the Youth Olympic Games.
Semifinal: Tanvi holds her nerve against Japan's second seed
The semifinal against Japan's second-seeded Yuzuno Watanabe proved to be a much tougher examination.
Tanvi began confidently, taking the opening game 21-14 with an aggressive approach and precise shot-making. However, Watanabe responded strongly in the second game, capitalising on Tanvi's errors to level the contest with a 21-11 win.
With a place in the final on the line, the Indian youngster needed to produce her best badminton in the deciding game. She managed to regain control of the rallies, improved her attacking approach and kept her composure in the closing stages.
In a closely contested decider, Tanvi edged past Watanabe 21-19 to book her place in the gold-medal match.
The victory was another landmark moment, making her the first Indian woman to reach a badminton final at the Youth Olympics.
Joins elite company of Indian badminton medallists
Tanvi's silver medal also adds to India's growing legacy in badminton at the Youth Olympic Games. She joins H.S. Prannoy, who won silver in 2010, and Lakshya Sen, who secured silver in 2018, as Indian badminton players to have reached the podium at the prestigious multi-sport event.
More importantly, her achievement marks a first for Indian women's badminton at the tournament.

briefs.headline: Urvil warms up for Mushtaq Ali Trophy in style
briefs.deck: The game-changing unbeaten 210 off just 227 balls was the cornerstone of Gujarat’s massive win over Kerala
briefs.bodyText:
Urvil Patel arguably made an early switch to white-ball mode ahead of the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy (SMAT) as he blasted a whirlwind double century against Kerala in the Ranji Trophy at the Narendra Modi Stadium.
The game-changing unbeaten 210 off just 227 balls was the cornerstone of Gujarat’s massive innings and 64-run win against Kerala and served as a perfect warm up for Urvil for the upcoming T20 tournament.
Kerala never recovered from Urvil’s brutal assault. It was a definitive statement knock from Urvil, who previously had showcased his big-hitting prowess for Chennai Super Kings in the IPL.
“It was my maiden double century in First Class cricket and I am happy that it came in a winning cause. I am always an aggressive batter and I love to play my strokes. When I came in we were in a spot of bother but I didn’t want the bowlers to dominate me, so I decided to attack. It was important to get a partnership going and Vishal (Jayswal) played beautifully,’’ he said.
“Kerala spinners were getting into a fine rhythm so I decided to attack and I took my chances against Aditya Sarvate. To be honest we didn’t want to bat again on this pitch so we needed to post a big total and it was important for me to continue batting till the end. It is a good win for us. I hope to carry this form into SMAT and help my side win the tournament,’’ he added.

briefs.headline: Kohli 2.0 - more dangerous, feared and destructive
briefs.deck: There is a ruthless streak about him, a burning desire to stamp his dominance from the get-go; he is primed for one final shot at another 50-over World Cup winner’s medal in the Africas next year
briefs.bodyText:
Virat Kohli is at that stage of his career where he is thoroughly enjoying himself. It’s not as if he isn’t as driven as previously; it’s just that, having shouldered the burden of the Indian batting for so long, he feels he has earned the right to express himself with greater freedom than ever before, especially considering the wealth of batting riches at India’s disposal in white-ball iterations.
This freeing up of the mind in the last year and a half has manifested itself in a new, exciting, exhilarating, compelling Virat Kohli. Just when we thought we had seen it all when it came to Kohli, a senior international for 18 years now, he shook us out of our complacent slumber, uncorking an avatar that is even more attractive and authoritative. As if that were possible, you ask? It most certainly is.
This gentle yet significant tweak in mindset coincided, for want of a better term, with his retirement from Test cricket in May 2025. After a forgettable tour of Australia – an unbeaten century in the second innings of the first Test in Perth turned out to be a false dawn, as he repeatedly was snared into edging the ball behind the stumps for the rest of the series – he pulled the plug on his Test odyssey midway through IPL 2025. Only Kohli can tell us if the subsequent deliberate shift in approach had anything to do with his Test retirement; Kohli doesn’t talk to us these days, not having attended a press conference for more than three years, so we can only speculate on that count.
